title: Wang Rong Xuan’s grandfather
excerpt: He and his wife ran a garment workshop in Fujian. Their children’s schooling took the family to Xiamen.

interview.recording: One interview recorded in three parts
interview.consent_note: For review. The narrator has not yet approved publication of his name, voice or transcript.

bio: He and his wife moved their garment workshop to Anhai for trade. Their children’s schooling took them to Xiamen, first separating the family and later leaving the parents with a daily commute.

route.note: Wang Rong Xuan mentions Shanghai, Hong Kong and overseas destinations. This part of the family’s history needs a separate interview.

question.text: Why did the family move to Anhai, and later to Xiamen?
question.note: Anhai offered better conditions for the workshop. In Xiamen, his priority was the children’s education.

chapters.title: Making clothes
body: He and his wife started making clothes in their home village. She did the sewing; he bought fabric and handled the business. When fabric was hard to find, he approached older state-owned factories to ask them to produce it.
Most of the clothes he remembers people wearing were dark. For summer, he wanted lighter fabric dyed in bright colours.

clip.zh: 人家穿衣都是深色的：什么枣红啊，什么黑色，什么咖啡。……我要的就是那个鲜艳。
clip.en: People wore dark colours: jujube red, black, coffee brown. … What I wanted was something bright.

chapters.title: The workshop in Anhai
body: Their children were already at school in the Anhai area when the couple decided to move the workshop there. He found it hard to do business in the village. Anhai had better roads and more trade, and it was easier to find out what was happening elsewhere.

clip.zh: 搬到安海镇，一心一心，一直奔往，一直向往前进。希望能改变，改变自己当时要创业的环境和条件。
clip.en: Moving to Anhai, we kept thinking of going forward. We hoped to change the surroundings and conditions we had for starting a business.

chapters.title: A home in Xiamen
body: They bought a flat in Xiamen so the children could go to school there. He thought the city offered a better education and a better environment. A written summary supplied with the recording dates the purchase to the 1990s; the year has not been confirmed.

Wang Rong Xuan’s father and aunt went to school in Xiamen. During high school, the father lived there on his own while his parents stayed at the factory in Jinjiang. The grandfather remembers the separation as difficult. He hoped the children would do well at school and that, one day, they would all be living together in Xiamen.
School names, entry requirements and fees are still unconfirmed.

clip.zh: 孩子们能送去学校是最好的，哪怕我们辛苦一点。
clip.en: Getting the children into school was the best thing, even if it meant more hardship for us.

chapters.title: Back to Jinjiang each morning
body: Eventually, he and his wife moved to Xiamen too. Every morning they drove back to the factory in Jinjiang and returned home at night. They kept this up for years.
He remembers how much the departure time mattered: leaving five minutes earlier could mean missing the traffic. The family still keeps the old Mercedes they drove to work.

clip.zh: 爷爷奶奶是每天早上从厦门（出发），去晋江上班，晚上再回来。好多年了，很多年了。
clip.en: Grandpa and Grandma left Xiamen for work in Jinjiang every morning, then came back at night. For years, for many years.

chapters.title: The plan for Shanghai
body: Shanghai was another place he had hoped to take the business. That move never happened. He says they did not have the conditions to go, but the recording does not make clear what was missing.

clip.zh: 去上海发展，但是也不够条件。……条件不够。
clip.en: To develop in Shanghai, but the conditions were not enough. … The conditions were not enough.

chapters.title: Looking back
body: When Wang Rong Xuan asks what the family gained and lost by moving, his grandfather says it was all gain.
He does not think young people must always strike out, though he believes the family should support them. He values health, family and contentment.

clip.zh: 幸福什么意思？就是今天出太阳，我感觉很开心；下雨，我也感觉很高兴。
clip.en: What does happiness mean? Today the sun is out and I feel glad; it rains and I still feel happy.

context.heading: Further reading
paragraphs: The teacher’s reading list includes Dorothy Solinger’s Contesting Citizenship in Urban China (1999). It may help with questions about the documents, fees and residence arrangements the family needed for schooling in Xiamen. These details are missing from the interview.

Vanessa Fong’s Paradise Redefined (2011) examines Chinese students studying abroad. It is a possible reference for a later interview about the younger generations. Their experiences outside Fujian have not yet been recorded here.
references: Solinger, Dorothy J. 1999. Contesting Citizenship in Urban China: Peasant Migrants, the State, and the Logic of the Market. University of California Press. Publisher.
Fong, Vanessa L. 2011. Paradise Redefined: Transnational Chinese Students and the Quest for Flexible Citizenship in the Developed World. Stanford University Press. Catalogue.

method_notes: The interview was recorded in three parts: 16:05, 07:35 and 12:08. This page uses six excerpts. The originals are preserved locally.
The date, place and full list of people present are unconfirmed. The grandmother is mentioned as present, and another voice may be heard.

The Chinese transcript was prepared from Breeze-ASR-26 output and an accompanying written summary. On 10 October 2026, the six excerpts and selected uncertain passages were compared with Qwen3-ASR-1.7B output. A Hokkien speaker still needs to check the recording.
The English translation and editorial text were drafted with AI assistance and await review by the interviewer and family. The written summary’s author is unconfirmed.

The home village and the year of the Xiamen flat purchase remain uncertain. The car’s mileage is discussed as both 600,000 and 400,000 kilometres, ending with “400,000-something”; the speaker and figure need checking. Neither figure establishes the distance driven for work. A passage about character in part 3 is also unclear.
The narrator has not yet approved publication. Sensitive or unclear passages need his review.
